title: Boosting Performance in Universal Allocation: Tips, Best Practices & New Features
author: Eugen_Simandel
text:
Universal Allocation is SAP's unified, user-friendly solution for overhead cost allocation in SAP S/4HANA. Born out of a vision to modernize a process that once spanned over 120 separate transactions across four sub-ledgers, Universal Allocation now delivers 9 SAP Fiori applications that cover the full spectrum of allocation scenarios — from simple cost-center cycles to complex profitability distributions. Its ambition is to bring the allocation process into the 21st century, offering not only rule maintenance and run processing, but also a rich analytics portfolio and, looking ahead, an agentic AI toolset. 
 But as any practitioner knows, performance can become a real challenge when allocation landscapes grow in complexity. In a recent Live Learning Session, product experts Eugen Simandel and Adam Vitek shared a structured overview of where performance issues arise, how to prevent them, and what SAP is actively building to address them. This article distills those insights into a practical guide.

title: Notes on fine-tuning a local model for agentic ABAP
author: erhankeseli
text:
This is a private project in my free time. The opinions are my own. 
 Summary 
 I took an open-weight model (Qwen3.6-35B-A3B) and trained it on ABAP code and documentation. It runs on a Mac with 48 GB of memory. 
 On my test of 11 agentic ABAP tasks, the mean score went from 31 to 59 with training, and to 73 with 8 working rules in the system prompt. 
 In a pilot, the model wrote a small application from a design document (2 classes, 1 report, 26 unit tests) while a large cloud model did the orchestration. All tests passed. 
 I do not publish the model at this time, because it is not mature. 
 Why I did this 
 I use large cloud models for ABAP development every day. They are good, but the expensive part of my work is not the thinking. It is the volume: when the design is clear, a model must write many methods and unit tests. I wanted to know if a small local model can do this part. 
 The model must work as an agent. It does not only print code. It creates objects on an ABAP system, writes the source, activates it, reads the error messages and runs the unit tests. 
 The setup 
 ABAP system: Self hosted 
 Tools: My self developed MCP server, which runs as an Eclipse plugin ( EPOD ABAP MCP Server ). The model gets about 20 tools: search, read source, write source, activate, run unit tests, and more. 
 Hardware: Two (ABAP AS + HANA) HomeLab servers for the ABAP system and the test harness, and a Mac Mini (M4 Pro, 64 GB) as the model server with MLX. 
 Base model: Qwen3.6-35B-A3B, a mixture-of-experts model with 35 billion parameters, of which 3 billion are active for each token. I use a 6-bit build. 
 Training: NVIDIA DGX Spark. 
 The test 
 The test has 11 tasks: classes with unit tests, function modules, reports and CDS views. Each task runs 3 times, so one measurement is 33 runs and takes about 5 hours. 
 The scoring is strict. If an object is not active at the end, or if the model changes an object that it must not change, the score of the run is 0. Hidden unit tests give the rest of the score. 
 One important number: with 33 runs, the difference between two measurements has a noise of about 6 points. A gain of 4 points means nothing. 
 What the training did 
 I did not train on chats or on tool calls. I trained on raw text only: ABAP source code and documentation. This is called continued pretraining. 
 Step Mean score Runs that the model ended itself 
 Base model 30.9 9 of 33 
 Round 1: ABAP source code and documentation (9 million tokens) 53.8 15 of 33 
 Round 2: + 4,100 verified sources (5 million tokens) 59.4 26 of 33 
 Round 2 + 8 working rules in the system prompt 72.9 22 of 33 
 The verified sources of round 2 came from an earlier experiment. A large model solved about 2,000 small ABAP tasks. I kept only the code that was active and passed its tests. 
 The largest effect of round 1 was on function modules. The base model wrote the parameter interface as a comment block, as in SE37. ADT does not accept this form. The trained model writes the parameters in the FUNCTION statement. 
 What did not work 
 I think this part is more useful than the table above. 
 More code of the same type. Round 2 added 5 million tokens of verified code. The gain was 3.7 points, which is inside the noise. 
 Repair examples. In round 3, I added about 1,300 examples of this form: source with an error, the error message of the system, the corrected source. The model did not get better at the correction of errors. "Field X is unknown" stayed at 16 % corrected. 
 Other base models. A dense 27B model was better on paper, but it made 9 tokens for each second on my Mac Mini. One turn took 30 minutes. A second candidate with the same size as my model wrote code with many simple syntax errors. 
 An earlier attempt with supervised fine-tuning on complete agent conversations gave no clear progress. 
 After round 1, training on raw text stopped at a mean of 55 to 60. The points that were lost after that were not ABAP knowledge. They were agent behaviour: what to do after an error message, which objects to touch, when to stop and ask. 
 What worked without training 
 The system prompt of my test had 259 tokens. I added 8 short rules, for example: 
 Change only the objects that the task tells you to create or to change. 
 After an activation error, read the message and the line that it names. Change only that part. Do not push the same source again. 
 If a business rule is missing, do not create an object. Stop and ask. 
 The mean went from 59.4 to 72.9, with no training. 
 A caution: I wrote the rules after I saw the failures on these 11 tasks. On new tasks the gain can be smaller. 
 The pilot: the local model as implementer 
 My real use is this: a large model makes the decisions and splits the work, and a cheaper model writes the code. So I measured this. 
 I wrote a design document for a small application on the flight demo tables: 2 classes with 10 methods, 1 report, 26 unit tests. All decisions were in the document. A large cloud model was the orchestrator. It gave each unit to the implementer, checked the result on the system, and sent the unit back if a check failed. 
 Local model as implementer Small cloud model as implementer 
 Work done, all tests pass yes yes 
 Units sent back 2 0 
 Code written by the orchestrator none none 
 Time 23 minutes 3.8 minutes 
 The limits 
 This is an experiment, not a product. 
 The test has only 11 tasks, and the pilot is one design document with one run. 
 The model corrects only about 37 % of its failed tool calls in the next turns. 
 Long reports fill the context, because each correction sends the full source again. 
 The same task can get 0 in one run and 90 in the next run. 
 The model needs a person or a larger model that checks its work. 
 What I learned 
 Training on raw ABAP text gives a large gain one time. It needs only a few hours on one GPU, and it does not damage the tool use of the model. 
 After that, more text does not help. The problems are behaviour, not knowledge. 
 A few clear working rules in the prompt gave more than two training rounds. 
 Measure the noise of your test before you believe a result. 
 Define the real use before you define the test. I measured autonomous work for 4 days. My real use is an implementer with a supervisor, and that is an easier job. 
 Why I do not publish the model 
 The model is not mature. The limits above are the reason. I want to see it do reliable work before I give it to other people. 
 What is next 
 A harness change that removes old copies of a source from the conversation, so that long reports do not fill the context. 
 A larger pilot with more than one design document. 
 More memory. A larger model on the same pipeline is the obvious next test. 
 If you do similar work, or if you want details about the test harness or the training setup, write a comment.

title: Autonomous Spend Management - An Overview
author: Abhijit_Shinde
text:
The vision of Autonomous Enterprise was unveiled at SAP Sapphire in May 2026 and expanded at SAP Connect in October 2026. It is SAP's unified vision and product architecture for running AI-native business operations. Rather than treating AI as isolated chatbots or add-ons, it embeds autonomous AI agents directly into core enterprise workflows - shifting human roles from manual execution to strategic direction and oversight. 
 Autonomous Spend Management is a key business domain of SAP's Autonomous Enterprise vision, transforming procurement from traditionally manual, transaction-driven processes into intelligent, AI-powered operations. 
 The purpose of this post is to provide an overview of the Autonomous Spend Management domain within SAP's Autonomous Enterprise vision based on my understanding. It could help readers understand the capabilities and prepare for its adoption.

title: Missão cumprida! Até 2027: SITCWB2026 celebra a força da comunidade SAP em Curitiba
author: SimoneKersck
text:
No último sábado, 7 de novembro, Curitiba foi palco de mais um capítulo especial da história da SAP Community. Realizamos a 4ª edição do SAP Inside Track Curitiba (SITCWB2026), um encontro que reuniu 440 inscritos e teve seus ingressos esgotados um mês antes do evento. Um sucesso absoluto que reforça o quanto nossa comunidade está viva, engajada e crescendo a cada ano! 
 Como parte da equipe organizadora e curadora da SAP Community Curitiba, é difícil colocar em palavras a alegria e o orgulho de ver tudo aquilo que construímos juntos se materializar. Cada edição tem sua própria história, e este ano não foi diferente. 

 Um dia de conhecimento, conexão e muita alegria 
 O dia começou com aquela energia que já é marca registrada do nosso SITCWB. Os participantes foram recebidos com muito carinho pela nossa equipe de voluntários, um delicioso coffee break e, neste ano, uma novidade que conquistou todos os corações: nossa capivara ganhou vida e se tornou a grande estrela da festa, trazendo ainda mais alegria e momentos especiais para o evento. 

 Também tivemos uma ativação no balcão da SAP Community Curitiba, fortalecendo a conexão dos participantes com a página oficial da SAP Community. Como parte dessa iniciativa, 200 participantes receberam uma caneca exclusiva do SITCWB2026. Mais do que um presente, uma lembrança de que fazemos parte de algo muito maior. 

 Outro momento muito especial foi: a Árvore da Comunidade. Cada participante foi convidado a escrever seu nome em uma folha e, juntos, fomos construindo uma árvore repleta de nomes. Mais do que uma atividade simbólica, essa iniciativa teve o propósito de representar o pertencimento, mostrando que cada pessoa é parte importante da nossa comunidade. Afinal, uma comunidade forte é construída por pessoas, e cada uma delas faz a diferença. Nossa árvore se tornou um símbolo lindo de conexão, união e da força que temos quando crescemos juntos. 

 A abertura foi um momento especial, conduzido por mim, Simone, ao lado do nosso curador @LuizSouza . Tivemos também a alegria de contar com a presença de quatro SAP Champions nesta edição ( @Marssel700 , @SimoneKersck , @RobertaFernande e @MustafaBensan ), tornando o encontro ainda mais significativo para a nossa comunidade. 

 E para conduzir essa jornada de conhecimento, contamos com nossos MCs @AdrianoCWB e Talis , que deram ritmo à programação, conectaram os diferentes momentos do evento e contribuíram para que tudo acontecesse de forma leve, dinâmica e acolhedora. 

 Na sequência, tivemos um momento especial com representantes da PUCPR, que compartilharam com os participantes um pouco sobre a estrutura, as oportunidades e tudo o que a instituição oferece, aproximando ainda mais a comunidade do ambiente acadêmico. 

 A partir daí, demos início a uma programação repleta de palestras enriquecedoras, compartilhamento de conhecimento, incluindo uma palestra internacional e diversas demonstrações que estimularam conversas, reflexões e novas possibilidades. 

 Ao longo do dia, tivemos experiências que tornaram o evento ainda mais especial. No intervalo do almoço, um picolé para refrescar e renovar as energias e uma ativação deliciosa da Pipoquinhas JP, que trouxe ainda mais sabor e alegria para o nosso encontro. São esses pequenos detalhes e experiências que ajudam a tornar cada edição única e especial. 

 Nos stands dos nossos patrocinadores Ouro, os participantes também puderam conhecer soluções, trocar experiências e ampliar seus conhecimentos. 

 E, claro, não poderia faltar aquilo que faz o SIT ser tão especial: o networking. Os encontros nos corredores, as conversas entre palestras, as novas conexões e os reencontros mostram que a comunidade SAP vai muito além da tecnologia. Ela é feita de pessoas. 
 A força de uma comunidade que cresce junto 
 O SITCWB2026 foi mais uma demonstração da força e do protagonismo da SAP Community em Curitiba. 
 Por trás de cada detalhe, existe uma equipe que acredita no propósito de compartilhar conhecimento, aproximar profissionais e criar oportunidades para que todos possam crescer juntos. 
 Meu agradecimento mais especial vai para os nossos voluntários. Vocês colocaram o coração em cada atividade, em cada recepção, em cada detalhe. A dedicação, o carinho e a energia de vocês fizeram toda a diferença. É impossível realizar um evento dessa dimensão sem pessoas tão comprometidas e especiais. 

 Aos nossos MCs Adriano e Talis, muito obrigada por conduzirem a programação com energia, carisma e dedicação. Vocês foram fundamentais para tornar a experiência do SITCWB2026 ainda mais leve, dinâmica e especial. 
 Aos palestrantes, nossa gratidão por compartilharem conhecimento, experiências e aprendizados tão valiosos. Vocês inspiram profissionais, despertam novas ideias e fortalecem o protagonismo de cada pessoa na construção de sua carreira. 
 À PUCPR, nosso reconhecimento por nos receber mais uma vez e compartilhar com a comunidade as oportunidades e a estrutura da instituição. 
 Aos nossos patrocinadores e apoiadores, muito obrigada por acreditarem no SITCWB e na força da comunidade. O apoio de vocês é fundamental para que possamos continuar realizando encontros como este, de forma colaborativa e com cada vez mais qualidade. 

 E também nosso carinho e agradecimento à Pipoquinhas JP por fazer parte dessa experiência e contribuir para deixar nosso encontro ainda mais especial. 
 E a todos que estiveram conosco, o nosso muito obrigada! Vocês são a razão de tudo isso acontecer. Cada conexão, cada troca e cada sorriso fizeram do SITCWB2026 um dia inesquecível. 
 Reviva os melhores momentos do SITCWB2026 
 Esta foto representa muito mais do que um evento: representa uma comunidade que cresce, se fortalece e constrói junto. 

 E para reviver toda essa energia, preparamos um registro especial de tudo o que aconteceu nesta edição. 
 🎬 Confira o After Movie do SITCWB2026: 
 https://youtu.be/ib__DaAYUQo 
 Missão cumprida! Até 2027! 
 Encerrar mais uma edição do SITCWB traz aquela mistura de felicidade, gratidão e saudade. Foram meses de planejamento, dedicação, desafios e muito trabalho, mas ver tudo se concretizar e sentir a energia de vocês faz cada esforço valer a pena. 
 Saímos desta edição com o coração cheio e a certeza de que estamos construindo algo muito especial. 
 A expectativa para 2027 já começou! Que venha mais um ano de aprendizado, conexões, colaboração e crescimento. 
 Porque a SAP Community Curitiba é isso: pessoas que compartilham, que apoiam, que acreditam e que fazem acontecer. 
 Missão cumprida, SITCWB2026! Nos vemos em 2027!

title: India’s Rise: From Promise to Platform for Global Growth
author: Paul Taylor
text:
India’s emergence is not a single story of growth, but a set of connected shifts changing how global companies think about markets, talent, technology, and innovation. 

 India today is an industrial and technology powerhouse, and it has become a strategic center for global business, technology, innovation, and investment. For SAP, that makes India not only an important domestic market, but also a place where enterprise technology is built, tested, and scaled for global impact. 

 The forces behind India’s rise are structural, not cyclical: economic scale, deep technology talent, and digital infrastructure built for mass adoption. Together, they have shifted India from a market companies serve or source from into one where global technology strategy is designed, tested, and scaled. 
 President and MD of SAP India Manish Prasad: “Touch any growth lever in India and you’ll find SAP there” 

 Read the interview 

 A $5 trillion economy 

 India’s growth, demographic scale, engineering talent, digital infrastructure, and expanding technology capabilities have set the pace for global growth and enterprise digital transformation. 

 India is already one of the fastest-growing major economies, with annual GDP growth of roughly 6.5% to 7% and an economy of about US$4.15 trillion today. 

 At its present growth rate, India is on track to cross the $5 trillion threshold shortly and become the world’s third-largest economy, overtaking Japan and Germany. By the end of the decade, India’s GDP is expected to be between $6 trillion and $7 trillion. 

 These are more than numerical milestones. A market of India’s size already influences global investment priorities, supply chain decisions, technology adoption, and corporate growth strategies. 

 Several structural advantages support this growth: a large domestic market with a population of 1.4 billion, rising affluence, and rapid urbanization that is increasing demand for infrastructure, housing, transportation, financial services, healthcare, and consumer products. 

 Government policy has reinforced this momentum through tax changes, foreign direct investment rules, production-linked incentives, and sustained infrastructure investment in ports, highways, logistics corridors, and renewable energy. 

 India’s $5 Trillion Rise is Changing Everything

 Video by Natalie Hauck and Alexander Januschke 

 Capital investment 

 At the same time, manufacturing investment has expanded as multinational companies have sought to diversify global supply chains and establish alternatives to excessive dependence on China and other production centers. 

 As incomes rise, consumption has expanded; as investment has increased, productivity has improved; and as productivity has improved, India has become more attractive to global capital. This feedback loop is giving the economy its own growth momentum while deepening its integration with global markets. 

 This shift has also changed how global executives view India. Companies that once treated India as a back-office or low-cost manufacturing base are now recalibrating it as a demand market, innovation hub, and source of global momentum. 

 A talent engine like no other 

 With more than one billion citizens under 35 and more than 2.5 million STEM graduates each year, India has one of the world’s deepest reservoirs of technology talent. That talent spans engineering, computer science, data science, mathematics, and applied sciences, feeding industries such as software engineering, semiconductor design, cloud infrastructure, cybersecurity, and artificial intelligence. 

 India’s universities, including the world-renowned IIT network, are also evolving. The IndiaAI Mission, launched in March 2024 with a budget of about $1.1 billion, supports AI research, compute infrastructure, and skills development so India can build AI systems, not just operate them. 

 This talent depth changes the calculus for global employers. It allows companies to staff large engineering initiatives at a scale that is difficult to match in most markets, making India a preferred location for next-generation engineering and innovation functions. 

 A full-stack digital nation 

 India’s digital transformation has provided another distinctive advantage: digital identity, payments, financial services, government platforms, and expanding connectivity built at national scale. This has created an environment where digital products can reach hundreds of millions of users quickly, giving companies a vast, real-world laboratory for new technologies and business models. 

 The country has long been a preferred offshore location for multinationals’ software and services work, now concentrated in Global Capability Centers. Over half of the world’s dedicated GCCs are located in India, where they employ nearly 2.1 million professionals and account for about 45% of major-city commercial office leasing. 

 These centers, which are expected to generate about $100 billion in export revenues this year, no longer simply provide back-office support. They have become full-stack innovation hubs running software development, product engineering, data analytics, cybersecurity operations, and AI and machine learning initiatives for their parent organizations. 

 Global banks like JP Morgan, technology giants including Google and Microsoft, and hundreds of others run mission-critical digital transformation programs out of India, not because it is the cheapest option, but because it has become one of the most capable. 

 This shift from cost arbitrage to capability arbitrage defines India’s current GCC boom. It shows that India has become a place where the world’s largest enterprises build and test their digital future, not merely maintain outsourced systems. 

 AI-ready by design 

 India also has the four conditions needed to become a leading artificial intelligence economy : data at scale, developer depth, compute investment, and a favorable policy framework. 

 First, data volume: more than a billion people generate data across payments, e-commerce, telecommunications, and government digital services, creating a critical input for training and refining AI systems at scale. 

 Second, the developer ecosystem: India has one of the world’s largest software developer populations, with a growing share focused on AI and machine learning and supported by a vibrant startup environment. 

 A recent GitHub report found that India added more than 5.2 million developers in one year, accounting for one in three new developers on the platform worldwide and is the second-largest contributor to GitHub AI projects. 

 Third, investment: AI startup funding rose sharply in 2025 across large language models, enterprise tools, and sector-specific applications. The IndiaAI Datasets Platform is also building public and private datasets for developers. 

 Fourth, regulation: India’s policy framework for data protection and AI governance is maturing toward a model that aims to balance innovation with accountability rather than defaulting to either extreme. 

 The strategic takeaway 

 Together, these factors position India not just to adopt AI built elsewhere, but to shape how AI and AI agents are built, deployed, and scaled globally. For example, India has become central to SAP’s AI strategy. Today over 80% of SAP’s AI agents are built in India, and India itself is one of SAP’s fastest-growing markets . 

 India’s emergence as a global economic and technological superpower is a reality. Its economy is growing faster than peers at comparable scale, its talent base is among the world’s deepest, its digital infrastructure is proven, and its AI ecosystem is moving from adoption to innovation. 

 Moving forward, India’s success will depend on how effectively it converts scale into productivity, talent into innovation, and digital infrastructure into globally competitive businesses while managing social and other challenges. The foundations are in place; the next decade will show whether India’s remarkable emergence as one of the world’s largest economies and principal engines of economic and technological growth can be sustained.
